extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of political theory, citizens and policymakers interested in democratic institutions
extracted.subtask_description: Extracting and evaluating the distinctive features, strengths, and dangers of democratic institutions (as described by Tocqueville) — e.g., respect for law, majority power, civic activity, instability of legislation, and safeguards against tyranny.

rubrics_metrics.name: Respect for the law (popular origin and parental affection)
rubrics_metrics.description: Respect of the Americans for the law—Parental affection which they entertain for it—Personal interest of everyone to increase the authority of the law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When the people are consulted in forming laws, the authority of the law is much augmented: popular origin 'contributes prodigiously to increase its power.' Citizens often view legislation with a kind of parental affection and obey not only because laws are the work of the majority, but because they 'originate in his own authority' and are regarded as a self-imposed contract. Anti-patterns: classes that did not participate in formation of law (slaves, paupers) feel less attachment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authority gained from popular origin
rubrics_metrics.description: It cannot be denied that, when the whole people can be consulted in legislation, the authority of the law is greatly increased.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Popular origin may impair legislative wisdom but massively increases obedience and legitimacy: 'There is an amazing strength in the expression of the determination of a whole people.' Political actors therefore strive to show they represent a majority. Example: parties claiming that the 'true majority abstained' to justify claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Personal interest in enforcing obedience
rubrics_metrics.description: In the United States everyone is personally interested in enforcing the obedience of the whole community to the law; the minority may soon rally the majority so it is in each person's interest to respect decrees they may need later.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The reciprocity of potential future power creates incentives to comply even with irksome enactments: laws are 'self-imposed evils' and 'evils of transient duration.' This personal stake functions as a social mechanism for compliance and stability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Breadth of the franchise as a source of legitimacy
rubrics_metrics.description: Except slaves, servants, and paupers in receipt of relief, there is no class in the United States that does not exercise the elective franchise and indirectly contribute to making the laws.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Wide participation strengthens the law's authority but also means opponents of laws must either change public opinion or disregard the people's decision. Note the caveat that exclusions (slaves etc.) produce inequalities in practice: formal rights may exist but social pressures can prevent exercise (example: freed blacks legally allowed to vote yet too intimidated to appear at polls).

rubrics_metrics.name: Class attitudes toward the law (wealthy suspicion vs. popular obedience)
rubrics_metrics.description: Because the European scale of authority is inverted in America, the wealthy often view the law with suspicion while poorer classes are its authors and defenders.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The rich may dread majority abuses and feel sullen dissatisfaction, but their wealth both prevents them from making law and from resisting it; thus they submit. Implication: social status shapes attitudes toward legislative authority and risk of unrest is concentrated among those with nothing to lose.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pervasive political activity and civic engagement
rubrics_metrics.description: Great activity pervades the United States: meetings at every level, debates, societies (e.g., temperance), frequent elections and local deliberations—political agitation extends into all social intercourse.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This ceaseless agitation trains citizens in public business, expands their ideas, and creates habits of participation (women attending meetings, debating clubs as entertainment). It also produces indirect social benefits (commercial activity). Anti-pattern: if citizens confined to private life they would be 'robbed of one half of his existence.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Democracy's indirect stimulation of commercial and social energy
rubrics_metrics.description: Democratic institutions, joined to the physical constitution of the country, are the (indirect) cause of prodigious commercial activity and of an all-pervading restless energy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The people learn how to promote commerce by experience derived from legislation; political participation diffuses skills and ambitions that fuel private enterprise. Note: Tocqueville distinguishes indirect (social) causes from direct legal inducements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quantity vs. quality of democratic government action
rubrics_metrics.description: Democracy may perform fewer things with great skill than some individual governments, but it does a greater number of things overall.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Democratic administration is less regular and methodical; it often abandons projects before fruition or risks them carelessly. Nevertheless, by mobilizing many actors it produces more activity and more initiatives than absolute governments. Tradeoff to evaluate: breadth of activity versus consistency and technical competence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moral authority of the majority (assumed infallibility)
rubrics_metrics.description: The moral authority of the majority rests partly on the notion that a great number is wiser than a single individual and that equality applies to intellect as well.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This doctrine encourages submission: human pride is assailed and the minority slowly yields. The authority of the many also gains sanction from duration—'its laws are not respected until they have long been maintained.' Danger: belief in majority infallibility contributes to intolerance of minority views.

rubrics_metrics.name: Formal and customary devices that increase majority power
rubrics_metrics.description: Most American constitutions and practices have artificially increased the natural strength of the majority (direct elections, short terms, pledged delegates, elective judges, legislature controlling judges' stipends).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Legal design choices (immediate election, brief terms, delegates pledged to follow elector instructions) and customs (Electors imposing lines of conduct) make legislatures highly susceptible to majority passions. Example: judges made dependent by legislative control of pay; delegates bound to promises from electors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mutability and instability of legislation and administration
rubrics_metrics.description: The omnipotence of the majority and rapid replacement of representatives increases the natural mutability of laws; America is the country where laws last the shortest time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Frequent constitutional amendments and legislative activity (e.g., Massachusetts' voluminous acts) produce a high turnover of laws. Administrative projects are started zealously but often not sustained (prison reform: building new penitentiaries while old jails decay). Evaluation criterion: durability and follow-through of public measures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tyranny of the majority and limits of popular sovereignty
rubrics_metrics.description: Although authority originates with the majority, the people do not have a right to do whatsoever they please; a general law of Justice, accepted by mankind, bounds their actions—otherwise majority may become tyrannical toward minorities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tocqueville warns that aggregating people does not change character; a collective majority can commit injustices like an individual despot. Remedies: recognize universal justice (appeal to 'sovereignty of mankind') and erect barriers preventing absolute majoritarian rule. Example: Baltimore mob attacking a newspaper and subsequent acquittal of guilty parties as majority tyranny.

rubrics_metrics.name: Need for institutional checks (independent legislature, executive, judiciary)
rubrics_metrics.description: To avoid tyranny, legislative power should represent the majority without being a slave to its passions; executive should retain some uncontrolled authority; judiciary should remain independent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Precautions and constitutional design are necessary to control the majority's action. Tocqueville notes the United States lacked sure barriers against majority abuses in manners and circumstances even where law offered some protection. Evaluation: presence and effectiveness of separation of powers and insulation mechanisms (e.g., non-elective or tenure-protected judges, executive stability).

rubrics_metrics.name: Arbitrary authority of public officers under majoritarian control
rubrics_metrics.description: Because the majority controls both lawmaking and appointment mechanisms, public officers may be viewed as passive agents and entrusted with arbitrary authority to serve majority designs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish tyranny (law-based) from arbitrariness (officers using discretionary power). In the U.S. the majority's dominance over appointments and judicial remuneration fosters arbitrariness; officers exercise power 'within a certain sphere' but as tools of majority will. Evaluation: degree to which officials can act independently of current majority preferences.
